title: Lesson 14 - A2.3 Attack Vectors (Independent Study)
subject: Information Technology
bigQuestion: How can an attacker find a way into a network?

sections.heading: What is an attack vector?
sections.text: An attack vector is the route (path) or method an attacker uses to reach a system or a weakness.
points: Example: an attacker sets up a fake Wi-Fi hotspot with a trusted name. A student connects, and now the attacker can see their data
Application: a college has Wi-Fi, an internet connection, and routers and switches. Each one is a possible route into the network
This lesson covers three groups: wireless (A2.3.1), the internet connection (A2.3.2) and internal network devices (A2.3.3)

diagram.alt: A college network in the centre, with four routes in. Wireless: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, NFC and RFID. A fake access point pretending to be trusted. The internet connection through the modem or router. An internal device such as a switch, router or access point. One weak device in the middle can expose every device on the network.
diagram.caption: Every route into the network is a possible attack vector.

sections.heading: Threat, vulnerability or attack vector?

head: Term
Meaning
Example
rows: The danger: who or what wants to cause harm
Someone trying to steal student data
A weakness an attacker can use
A router that hasn't been updated
The route the attacker uses to reach the weakness

points: Think of a burglar: the burglar is the threat, a broken window lock is the vulnerability, and the window is the attack vector (the way in)

Check-in: malware is sent through a weak college Wi-Fi network to steal student data. Threat = the attacker trying to steal student data; vulnerability = the weak Wi-Fi security; attack vector = the Wi-Fi network

sections.heading: Wi-Fi: a route through the air
points: A fake access point pretends to be a trusted network
Weak security (no password or old encryption) lets the wrong people in
Eavesdropping: an attacker listens to data sent through the air
Deauthentication (deauth) attack, step 1: the attacker sends fake 'disconnect' messages (deauth frames)
Step 2: the device drops off the Wi-Fi
Step 4: while it reconnects, the attacker captures useful login (authentication) information
Key idea: the attacker is attacking the CONNECTION, not always the device itself

sections.heading: The internet connection (A2.3.2)
sections.text: The connection device links the college network to the internet. Think about the connection type (copper, fibre, Wi-Fi, cellular/5G) and the connection device. Attackers target it because it links the inside network to the outside world, almost every outside attack has to cross it, and a badly set-up or out-of-date device is an easy way in.

head: Copper cable
Optical fibre
rows: With physical access, the line can be tapped and data intercepted
Harder to tap, but with physical access it can still be spliced (cut into)
Cutting or damaging it stops the connection
Cutting it also stops the connection

points: Key idea: 'harder to attack' does NOT mean 'impossible to attack'. If fibre is hard to tap, attackers may go after a wireless link instead

sections.heading: Internet connection devices

head: Device
What it does
Risk
rows: Links the organisation to its internet provider (cable or fibre)
Gives internet access AND Wi-Fi inside the building
Default passwords, old firmware or weak encryption
Gets the internet through the mobile network
Default settings or missing security updates

points: Check-in: a shop's 5G router still uses the password printed on its label. That's a risk because anyone who sees the label, or looks up the default online, can log in and change its settings
An unpatched router is a risk even if users have strong passwords, because the attacker can exploit the firmware weakness instead of guessing passwords

sections.heading: Internal network access devices (A2.3.3)

head: Device
What it does
If it's taken over
rows: Sends data between networks, or parts of a network
Could redirect traffic, read data or help the attacker move deeper in
Connects devices together inside one part of the network
A compromised managed switch could let an attacker watch traffic or change port settings
Lets devices join the network using Wi-Fi
A rogue or badly set-up one can spread the network outside the building

points: Key idea: these sit in the MIDDLE of the network, so if one is taken over, MANY devices are affected

Stretch: a compromised network device can be more serious than one compromised laptop BECAUSE a switch or router connects many devices, WHICH MEANS the attacker can watch or redirect everyone's traffic, SO the organisation could suffer a much wider data breach

keyIdea: A threat needs a route in: the attack vector. Wireless links (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, NFC, RFID…), the internet connection and its devices, and internal routers, switches and access points are all routes, and one weak device in the middle of a network can put every device at risk.
flashcards: Attack vector
The route (path) or method an attacker uses to reach a system or a weakness.
Threat vs vulnerability vs attack vector
Threat = who/what wants to cause harm; vulnerability = the weakness; attack vector = the route in.
Burglar analogy
Burglar = threat; broken window lock = vulnerability; the window = attack vector.
Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11)
Wireless networking. Attacked with fake access points and eavesdropping.
Bluetooth
Short-range wireless for headphones and keyboards. Risks: unprotected pairing, malicious files.
Cellular (4G/5G)
Mobile networks. Risks: rogue base stations, SIM weaknesses.
Satellite link
Used by ships, planes and remote places. Long-distance signals can be intercepted.
Infrared (IR)
Used by TV remotes and older devices. Signals can be captured and replayed.
NFC
Near-field communication, used for contactless payments. Risks: skimming, relay attacks.
RFID
Used in door entry cards and tags. Risks: eavesdropping, cloning tags.
Fake (rogue) access point
A Wi-Fi hotspot pretending to be a trusted network, so the attacker can see connected users' data.
Eavesdropping
Listening to data sent through the air.
Deauthentication attack
Fake 'disconnect' frames knock a device off Wi-Fi; as it reconnects, the attacker captures login information.
Copper vs fibre
Copper = electrical signals, can be tapped; fibre = light pulses, harder to tap but can be spliced.
Why target the internet connection?
It links the inside network to the outside world, and almost every outside attack crosses it.
Modem / router-modem
Links the organisation to its internet provider. Risk: poor set-up or missing updates.
Wireless router
Gives internet access and Wi-Fi. Risks: default passwords, old firmware, weak encryption.
Firmware
The built-in software in a device such as a router or access point. It needs updating.
Router (internal)
Sends data between networks. If taken over: redirects traffic, reads data, helps attackers move deeper.
Switch
Connects devices in one part of a network. If compromised: attacker can watch traffic or change port settings.
Wireless access point
Lets devices join by Wi-Fi. A rogue or badly placed one can spread the network outside the building.
Why network devices matter
They sit in the middle of the network, so one compromised device affects many others.

o: A weakness that an attacker can use
quiz.e: Vulnerability = weakness. The route is the attack vector.

quiz.q: Which TWO are ways a device can connect to a network without a cable?
quiz.e: Also cellular, NFC, RFID, infrared and satellite.

o: The route or method an attacker uses to reach a system or weakness

quiz.q: In the burglar analogy, what is the attack vector?
quiz.e: Burglar = threat, broken lock = vulnerability, window = attack vector.

quiz.q: Which wireless vector do contactless bank cards use?
quiz.e: NFC (near-field communication). Risks: skimming and relay attacks.

quiz.q: Give one risk of leaving Bluetooth switched on in a public place.
o: It may accept unwanted connections or malicious files
quiz.e: Unprotected pairing can let attackers connect or send files.

quiz.q: Why can satellite signals be intercepted?
o: They are always unencrypted on purpose
They travel long distances through the air, so others can pick them up
quiz.e: Long-distance wireless signals cover a wide area.

quiz.q: In a deauthentication attack, what does the attacker send?
quiz.e: The device drops off, reconnects, and the attacker captures login information.

quiz.q: Why is optical fibre harder to tap than copper?
o: It carries data as light pulses, not electrical signals
quiz.e: Harder, but not impossible: it can still be spliced with physical access.

quiz.q: What does a modem / router-modem connect an organisation to?
quiz.e: It links the building to the internet provider.

quiz.q: Give two reasons a wireless router might be easy to attack.
o: It has strong encryption and updates

quiz.q: A student connects to a fake Wi-Fi access point. What attack vector is being used?
quiz.e: One risk: the attacker can see their data, including logins.

quiz.q: Why can an unpatched wireless router be a risk even if users have strong passwords?
o: Attackers can exploit the firmware weakness without needing passwords
quiz.e: The vulnerability is in the device itself.

quiz.q: A switch inside a college network is compromised. How could this affect other devices?
o: The attacker could watch their traffic or change port settings
quiz.e: Switches connect many devices, so one compromise affects them all.

quiz.q: Which internal device lets devices join the network using Wi-Fi?
quiz.e: A badly set-up one can spread the network outside the building.

quiz.q: Why do attackers target an organisation's internet connection?
o: It links the inside network to the outside world, and most outside attacks cross it
quiz.e: It's the main gateway in and out.

apply.title: Find the way in
apply.intro: Pick the attack vector, the type of term, or the best fix for each situation.

items.task: A criminal group wants to steal a hospital's patient records. Threat, vulnerability or attack vector?
items.e: Who or what wants to cause harm = threat.

items.task: A switch in the comms room hasn't had a firmware update for three years. Threat, vulnerability or attack vector?
items.e: A weakness an attacker can use = vulnerability.

items.task: Malware reaches a laptop through a Bluetooth connection left on in public. Threat, vulnerability or attack vector?
Someone copies the signal from an office door entry card and makes a clone.
items.e: RFID door cards can be eavesdropped on and cloned.

items.task: A hidden device near a till relays a contactless card payment to a criminal's reader.
items.e: NFC is used for contactless payments; relay attacks pass the signal on.

items.task: A fake mobile phone mast tricks nearby phones into connecting to it.
items.e: Cellular networks can be attacked with rogue base stations.

items.task: Students' laptops keep dropping off the Wi-Fi and reconnecting, and an attacker captures login data while they reconnect.
items.e: Fake disconnect frames force reconnection, exposing authentication information.

items.task: A shop's 5G router still uses the password printed on its label. What's the best fix?
o: Hide the label behind a poster
Move the router to the window
Change it to a strong, unique admin password and update the firmware
items.e: Default credentials are easy to find. Change them and keep the device updated.

items.task: A managed switch linking every office PC is in an unlocked cupboard. What's the risk?
o: An attacker could compromise it and watch or change traffic for all those PCs
items.e: Internal devices sit in the middle of the network, so many devices are affected.

items.task: An access point on an outside wall sends Wi-Fi into the car park. What's the risk?
o: Someone outside the building could try to connect to the network
The car park gets faster internet
items.e: A badly placed access point spreads the network outside the building.

items.task: Copper vs fibre: an attacker with physical access wants to intercept data most easily. Which cable is easier to tap?
items.e: Copper carries electrical signals and can be tapped; fibre is harder (but can be spliced).

items.task: Why can a compromised router be more serious than one compromised laptop?
o: The router connects many devices, so the attacker can redirect or read everyone's traffic
items.e: Internal devices sit in the middle of the network: one takeover affects many.

exam.q: 1(a). State what is meant by an attack vector.
pts: The route or method an attacker uses to reach a system or weakness

exam.q: 1(b). Give two wireless attack vectors, other than Wi-Fi.
pts: Any one: Bluetooth / cellular (4G/5G) / satellite / infrared / NFC / RFID
A second, different one from the list
exam.tip: Don't say Wi-Fi: the question rules it out.

exam.q: 1(c). Explain one reason why optical fibre is harder for an attacker to tap than copper cable.
pts: Fibre carries data as pulses of light, not electrical signals like copper
so the signal can't easily be intercepted by tapping the line; the cable would have to be spliced (cut into)

exam.q: 1(d). A school's wireless router still uses its default admin password. Explain why this is a vulnerability.
pts: Default passwords are printed on the device or published online, so they are easy to find or guess
which means an attacker could log in as admin and change settings, read traffic or get into the network
exam.tip: Why it's easy to find + what the attacker could then do.

exam.q: 2. State whether each describes a threat, a vulnerability or an attack vector. (i) A criminal group wants to steal a hospital's patient records. (ii) A switch in the comms room has not had a firmware update for three years. (iii) Malware reaches a laptop through a Bluetooth connection left on in public.
pts: (i) Threat
(ii) Vulnerability
(iii) Attack vector
exam.tip: Use the burglar analogy: who (threat), what weakness (vulnerability), which way in (attack vector).

exam.q: 3. Describe how a deauthentication attack can be used against a Wi-Fi network.
pts: The attacker sends fake 'disconnect' messages (deauthentication frames) to a device
The device drops off the Wi-Fi and then automatically reconnects
While it reconnects, the attacker captures login (authentication) information
exam.tip: "Describe" = the steps in order. 3 marks = 3 clear points.

exam.sc: A college has student Wi-Fi and staff Wi-Fi, a 5G backup router, several switches and wireless access points. One access point has old firmware and a weak admin password.
exam.q: Case study (a). Identify the attack vector and the vulnerability, explain one possible impact, and suggest one sensible security improvement.
pts: Attack vector: the wireless access point (Wi-Fi)
Vulnerability: old firmware and a weak admin password
Impact, e.g. an attacker takes over the access point and gets into the college network to watch traffic or steal student data
Improvement, e.g. update the firmware and set a strong, unique admin password
exam.tip: From the slides' college case study. One mark for each of the four parts.

exam.sc: A college has student Wi-Fi and staff Wi-Fi, a 5G backup router, several switches and wireless access points. One access point has old firmware and a weak admin password.
exam.q: Case study (b). Explain why a compromised internal network device can be more serious than one compromised laptop.
pts: Because a switch, router or access point connects many devices, while a laptop is just one
which means the attacker can watch, redirect or change traffic for every connected device
so the organisation could suffer a much wider data breach or disruption
exam.tip: The slides' stretch task: Because… which means… so the organisation could…

exam.sc: Meridian Parcels is a courier company with 60 staff and a busy warehouse. Broadband comes in over an old copper line to a modem-router, which still uses the default admin password on its label. Drivers connect company tablets to an open guest Wi-Fi network. Staff use RFID swipe cards to enter the warehouse; some cards are over 10 years old. One managed switch, in an unlocked cupboard, links every office computer. A wireless access point on an outside wall sends its signal into the staff car park.
exam.q: 4(a). Identify one wireless attack vector from the scenario.
pts: Any one: the open guest Wi-Fi / the RFID swipe cards / the wireless access point signal in the car park
exam.tip: "Identify" = pick it straight from the scenario.

exam.sc: Meridian Parcels is a courier company with 60 staff and a busy warehouse. Broadband comes in over an old copper line to a modem-router, which still uses the default admin password on its label. Drivers connect company tablets to an open guest Wi-Fi network. Staff use RFID swipe cards to enter the warehouse; some cards are over 10 years old. One managed switch, in an unlocked cupboard, links every office computer. A wireless access point on an outside wall sends its signal into the staff car park.
exam.q: 4(b). Identify one internal network access device that could be used as an attack vector.
pts: The managed switch (accept: the wireless access point)
exam.tip: Internal devices: router, switch, wireless access point.

exam.sc: Meridian Parcels is a courier company with 60 staff and a busy warehouse. Broadband comes in over an old copper line to a modem-router, which still uses the default admin password on its label. Drivers connect company tablets to an open guest Wi-Fi network. Staff use RFID swipe cards to enter the warehouse; some cards are over 10 years old. One managed switch, in an unlocked cupboard, links every office computer. A wireless access point on an outside wall sends its signal into the staff car park.
exam.q: 4(c). Explain one vulnerability of Meridian's modem-router.
pts: It still uses the default admin password printed on its label
so anyone who sees the label, or looks up the default online, could log in and change its settings or get into the network
exam.tip: Use the scenario's exact detail: 'the default admin password on its label'.

exam.sc: Meridian Parcels is a courier company with 60 staff and a busy warehouse. Broadband comes in over an old copper line to a modem-router, which still uses the default admin password on its label. Drivers connect company tablets to an open guest Wi-Fi network. Staff use RFID swipe cards to enter the warehouse; some cards are over 10 years old. One managed switch, in an unlocked cupboard, links every office computer. A wireless access point on an outside wall sends its signal into the staff car park.
exam.q: 4(d). The access point's signal reaches the staff car park. Describe how an attacker could use this to reach Meridian's systems.
pts: An attacker sits in the car park, within range of the Wi-Fi signal, without entering the building
They connect to, or attack, the network, e.g. eavesdropping, a deauthentication attack to capture logins, or a fake access point with the same name
Once connected, they can reach Meridian's internal systems and data
exam.tip: Describe the steps: get in range → attack the connection → reach systems.

exam.sc: Meridian Parcels is a courier company with 60 staff and a busy warehouse. Broadband comes in over an old copper line to a modem-router, which still uses the default admin password on its label. Drivers connect company tablets to an open guest Wi-Fi network. Staff use RFID swipe cards to enter the warehouse; some cards are over 10 years old. One managed switch, in an unlocked cupboard, links every office computer. A wireless access point on an outside wall sends its signal into the staff car park.
exam.q: 4(e). The IT manager says: "As long as the front door is locked, the network is safe." Explain two reasons why the IT manager is wrong.
pts: Reason 1: wireless signals go beyond the walls, e.g. the access point reaches the car park, or drivers use open guest Wi-Fi
so an attacker can reach the network without ever coming through the front door
Reason 2: the internet connection is an attack vector, e.g. the modem-router still has its default password
so attackers can get in remotely over the internet (also accept: old RFID cards could be cloned, or the switch is in an unlocked cupboard)
exam.tip: Two separate points, each with a reason, both using scenario details.
